source.title: Can We Gain More from Orthogonality Regularizations in Training Deep CNNs?
source.authors: Nitin Bansal; Xiaohan Chen; Zhang-Yang Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study applies explicit orthogonality regularizers during CNN training and reports held-out classification error, bearing on whether explicit regularization changes generalization performance. It does not test any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The study reports held-out error for orthogonality regularization conditions, which is explicit regularization but is not one of the specific interventions or measurements in V1–V8. Cited results about other studies were excluded.
record.test_reason: The study compares orthogonality regularizers using CNN classification error and convergence. These results test none of V1–V8. Different optimizers are used for different architectures, without a controlled optimizer comparison; spectral regularization is not a measurement of magnitude-aware sharpness. The discussion of sharp minima cites prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors advocate orthogonality regularization for better accuracy and faster, smoother convergence, with SRIP usually strongest and DSO sometimes worse than baseline. Their broad concluding language exceeds the uniformity of their table results. The effective recipe schedules orthogonality strength and changes weight-decay settings.
record.recipe_differences: Trains standard CNNs with added orthogonality regularizers and compares classification error; does not test arbitrary-label memorization, width sweeps, or train-test gaps.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by regularizer, model, and dataset. The authors report that switching the regularization coefficients during training improves final accuracy, and orthogonality's impact weakens and can become slightly negative near the end of training.

fits_no_version.finding: Orthogonality regularization often improves held-out CNN classification performance. For example, SRIP reduces Wide ResNet 28-10 CIFAR-100 error from 20.50% to 18.19%. DSO sometimes worsens error, and coefficient scheduling affects performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scheduled orthogonality regularization can improve CNN image-classification accuracy and convergence, with effects depending on the regularizer, architecture, and dataset.

record.problems: No training-error values or train-test gaps are reported, so the effect on the claimed gap cannot be assessed. Tabled comparisons do not report uncertainty except for the three-initialization stability statement; the numerical rows generally lack error bars.
record.rows_left_out: The cited Jacobian norm regularizer results are explicitly attributed to prior work, so they were not recorded as the study's own result. Figure 1 validation curves were not transcribed because the supplied text gives no numeric values and the authors' qualitative summary is covered in the excerpts.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization under the same recipe, and random-label held-out chance performance.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons and tuning sensitivity.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Adding or removing dropout, dropout strength, and training-set-size dependence.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Removing high-memorization examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain unlinked because the intervention and comparisons fall outside V1–V8, not merely because numerical generalization gaps are unavailable. The record also omits an own SRIP experiment: Wide ResNet 22-layer, width 5 achieves 4.28% CIFAR-10 error in Section 4.1. Its comparator values are cited, but this SRIP value is the study's own result; it still fits no listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization under controlled tuning.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

relation.reason: The related work discusses generalizability and Hessian-based arguments, but the study's experiments do not test the listed claim versions.

tranche.reason: The experiments compare orthogonality regularizers and classification performance; they neither test nor use any specific finding in V1–V8. Spectral regularization does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness.
